Description.Summary: Glean Agents is a closed-source enterprise AI agent platform that automates knowledge-work tasks (standup reports, code review, onboarding) by indexing company data from Slack, GitHub, and Jira. As of 2025, Glean processes 100M+ agent actions per year, employs 850+ people, and raised a $150M Series F at a $7.2B valuation.

Practices.Summary: Glean evaluates agents with curated evalsets of ~20 real-world examples graded on binary sub-metrics (completeness, tone, groundedness) under a single north-star metric, continuously refreshed with sampled user queries and upvote/downvote feedback.

evidence.quote: At Glean, we've been running large-scale evaluations for years, building on what we learned from search.

A good evaluation starts with an evalset: a representative set of user instructions paired with the ideal responses. The most impactful improvements to AI agents come from a structured feedback loop: refining instructions, structuring context, tuning model parameters, and selecting the right language models.
When it comes to grading metrics, simple binary scoring (0 or 1) works best. It avoids the confusion that comes with partial scores and keeps results clear and consistent.
You can even sample real user queries and add them to your evaluation to keep your evalset fresh and aligned with evolving user needs.

Practices.Summary: After each eval run, Glean engineers review failing examples for patterns, then apply fixes in a strict priority order: refine instructions first, then restructure context (point to specific sources, use sub-agents), then tune LLM parameters (e.g. temperature), and only swap the model last.

evidence.quote: Start by looking at the metrics to see where the agent underperformed, review examples to spot patterns, and then make targeted improvements.
As a rule of thumb, make agent changes in this order: Refine instructions... Structure context... Tune parameters... Choose LLMs.
A sales prospecting agent failing at personalization may not be using the right sources, so rewording its search instructions can help. If tone is the issue, add examples of good versus bad tone.

Practices.Summary: Glean advises building evalsets around complex, multi-step tasks first — not simple happy-path queries — because users routinely push agents across multiple sources and reasoning steps, making these the highest-value validation cases.

evidence.quote: Don't shy away from complex evalsets! Users tend to push the capabilities of agents by asking for multi-step tasks across multiple sources. These aren't edge cases, but often the most valuable jobs to be done.
Start by testing instructions you're unsure about to see exactly what your agent can handle before you dive into optimizations.

Tools.Summary: LLM-as-judge graders aligned to human SME feedback are used alongside continuously running platform-level metrics (accuracy, relevance, completeness, groundedness).

evidence.quote: Most of these are graded by LLMs aligned to user feedback such as upvotes and downvotes, as well as human subject matter experts.
Glean continuously runs platform-level evaluations in the background, tracking metrics like accuracy, relevance, and instruction following to ensure agents stay reliable at scale.
Alongside query sampling, automating grading using LLMs is a great way to scale your evaluations as your userbase grows.

Stakeholders.Summary: Evalsets are co-curated with internal subject-matter experts (e.g., the sales team for a sales-prospecting agent); grading involves both LLM judges and human SMEs.

evidence.quote: Start by asking a few user subject matter experts to help curate a small, high-quality set of about 20 real-world examples.
For example, when we built a sales prospecting agent, we asked the sales team what makes a great first-touch email.

Others.Summary: Glean treats AI workflow testing as distinct from deterministic QA, layering data-quality, model-quality, adversarial-robustness, and business-impact tests. Production ranking releases send a warmup request before switching configuration to avoid first-load latency.

evidence.quote: Testing AI automation workflows demands a fundamentally different approach than traditional software quality assurance.
Hence for production releases, we typically send a warmup request before switching the configuration.

Others.Summary: Glean's published benchmarks show Agentic Engine 2 achieved 94% task completeness, a 21% query increase in testing, and resolved 20% more of the hardest failing query types. AI safeguard models hit 97.8% / 93.5% / 94.3% accuracy on prompt injection, toxic content, and malicious code with a 3.0% false positive rate.

evidence.quote: Our new architecture achieved completeness scores of 94%, meaning that the engine accomplishes the full task you asked for, end-to-end.
When judged using human feedback from previously downvoted queries, Agentic Engine 2 was able to tackle 20% more of the most challenging query types that users ask Assistant.
This performance difference translated directly into increased usage — with a jump of 21% more queries run in Assistant during testing.
Glean achieves 97.8% accuracy on prompt injection detection, 93.5% accuracy on toxic content detection, and 94.3% on malicious code detection on leading benchmarks.

Practices.Summary: Glean built a custom dynamic-deployment mechanism that loads new Java Index Server versions from Cloud Storage without restarting, enabling nightly internal rollouts, weekly customer rollouts, and instant rollback via configuration change.

evidence.quote: We realized that much of the problem was solved if we could avoid restarting our Index Server to receive code updates in the common case.
Since server restarts were no longer normally needed, we started rolling out ranking changes more frequently—nightly for internal deployment, and weekly for customers.
Rolling back a problematic release could be done instantly with an online configuration change.

Stakeholders.Summary: The ranking team drove incremental deployment; their iteration speed was previously bottlenecked by 15+ minute Index Server preload times.

evidence.quote: To help build these features, we wanted frequent iterative releases for our ranking team.
And our engineers found that their development cadence was unnecessarily slowed down by long server restart times.

Others.Summary: Each release tag is isolated from other experiments and associated with its own errors, enabling strong versioning across simultaneously running code versions.

evidence.quote: Strong versioning: Errors could be associated with specific release tags, and different experiments were isolated from each other.

Others.Summary: Glean's hot-swap mechanism is built on custom Java ClassLoaders and ObjectWeb ASM for class-package remapping, loading JAR files from Cloud Storage in seconds. The platform is deployed in single-tenant isolated environments on AWS, Azure, or GCP.

evidence.quote: After looking into custom ClassLoaders, we prototyped loading a Java JAR archive from Cloud Storage and using the classes in our process, without a restart.
We used some open source libraries (e.g. ObjectWeb ASM) to help build this remapping tool.
Run Glean in a fully isolated, single-tenant environment that keeps your data and platform secure, either Glean-hosted or in your own AWS, Azure, or GCP cloud.

Practices.Summary: Glean's PR Review and Resolve GitHub PR Feedback agents scan code changes, flag risk areas, aggregate unresolved comments, and produce prioritized checklists to keep review quality consistent as the team scales.

evidence.quote: Pull request reviews remain one of the most common sources of delay. Reviewers need to understand code changes in context, assess alignment with design intent, and ensure consistency with existing standards.
The pull request review agent scans code changes, suggests improvements, and flags areas that may need closer attention to support faster, more consistent reviews.

The resolve GitHub PR feedback agent aggregates unresolved comments, classifies them by priority, and generates an actionable checklist with file references and relevant context so engineers can close out reviews faster.

Tools.Summary: GitHub is the code-review platform, augmented by Glean's own PR Review and Resolve GitHub PR Feedback agents.

evidence.quote: Engineering time rarely disappears in one big way. It gets lost in small, repeatable moments where context is scattered, handoffs are frequent, and progress depends on someone knowing where to look.
Glean accelerates software engineering workflows with context-aware agents that work across the systems engineers already use — repositories, tickets, documents, and communication tools.

Stakeholders.Summary: Distributed engineering reviewers; agents support reviewers rather than replace them, with humans still resolving threads.

evidence.quote: As teams scale, review quality becomes uneven and feedback cycles lengthen.

Issues.Description: AgentSeal adversarial scan flagged that people_profile_search exposes a broad set of employee PII (email, manager_email, department) in tool outputs, raising data-minimization concerns for the local MCP server.

Issues.Issue_Title: Your tool has been listed on the AEGIS Protocol skill registry
Issues.Description: External notification that @gleanwork/local-mcp-server was listed on the AEGIS Protocol on-chain trust and attestation registry for AI agent tools (Base Mainnet).

Issues.Issue_Title: [BUG] npx @gleanwork/local-mcp-server fails with EUNSUPPORTEDPROTOCOL for workspace:*
Issues.Description: Running `npx -y @gleanwork/local-mcp-server` fails with npm error EUNSUPPORTEDPROTOCOL: 'Unsupported URL Type "workspace:": workspace:*' — the published package leaks a pnpm workspace protocol dependency that npm cannot resolve.

Issues.Issue_Title: [FEATURE] Adopt provider-prefixed tool names for all exposed MCP tools to ensure clear namespacing
Issues.Description: When integrating multiple MCP servers from different providers, generic tool names cause namespace collisions. Request to adopt provider-prefixed tool names across all exposed Glean MCP tools.

The VSCode client supports `--workspace` to add Glean to workspace-scoped MCP servers, but the claude-code client only supports adding Glean to the global MCP server list — request for project-specific configuration parity.

Issues.Issue_Title: [BUG] Warnings in tests RE: requests without a request handler
Issues.Description: Test suite emits MSW warnings ('intercepted a request without a matching request handler') for unmocked OAuth authorization-server metadata requests in src/test/auth/authorize.test.ts, indicating incomplete request handler coverage.

Issues.Issue_Title: [FEATURE] Option to deploy MCP server as SSE
Issues.Description: In many corporate environments running local MCP servers is impractical. Request to create an SSE-based MCP that can be deployed via Docker to a Kubernetes cluster, with user auth handled through user config.
Follow-up to the new `configure` command (#38): support updating an existing MCP configuration when authentication credentials change, including a `--force` flag to overwrite current configuration.

Issues.Issue_Title: [P2] No test sandbox or record/replay for CI-friendly testing
Issues.Description: All development and testing in the glean-agent-toolkit runs against production Glean — there is no sandbox instance, no seed data, no record/replay mechanism, mock server, or dry-run flag available to users. CI/CD pipelines cannot test the knowledge layer without live production credentials; HTTP-level mocking is fragile and drifts on API changes.

Issues.Issue_Title: Google Workspace Custom Actions: oneOf schema issue + documentation contradiction
Issues.Description: Google Docs/Slides batch-update APIs use Protocol Buffer oneOf semantics (exactly one operation per request item), but Glean's published developer documentation defines mutually-exclusive request fields as sibling properties with no schema-level enforcement. The LLM populates both fields and Google rejects the call. Additionally, the 'no nested fields' guideline in the developer docs directly contradicts a published Glean example that nests objects 3-4 levels deep.

Issues.Issue_Title: Bug – Async path in adapter can block event loop
Issues.Description: The on_invoke_tool hook in the OpenAI adapter is declared async but calls the original tool function synchronously, with no detection of whether the function is a coroutine and no offloading. Under concurrent load, synchronous tools block the event loop, reducing throughput and causing latency spikes.

Practices.Summary: Public issues across glean-agent-toolkit and mcp-server reveal five recurring problem categories: security/PII exposure in tool outputs, package dependency leaks (workspace protocol in npm), configuration gaps (missing force-overwrite, no SSE deployment), absent CI test sandboxes requiring live production credentials, and schema or documentation inconsistencies causing API rejections.

evidence.quote: All development and testing currently runs against production Glean. There is no sandbox instance, no seed data, no record/replay, no mock server, no dry_run flag.

Google's batchUpdate APIs use Protocol Buffer oneof semantics. Each item in the requests array must contain exactly ONE operation type. The LLM sometimes populates both fields in one request item, which Google rejects.

Practices.Summary: Glean is model-agnostic, routing tasks to specialized LLMs by job type (code, image, research, routing). Prompt practice favors minimal system prompts; the recommended tuning order is instructions → context structure → parameters → model swap.

evidence.quote: At Glean, we already select different models for different jobs—image generation, code generation, deep research, lightweight routing—regardless of provider.
Like many others, we've found that with AI agents, minimizing system prompts, giving agents a clear menu of prioritized tools, and allowing early exploration leads to higher-quality results.
Tool names and descriptions evolve over time so that as tools are evaluated and new ones are added, they continue to perform optimally.
As a rule of thumb, make agent changes in this order: Refine instructions... Structure context... Tune parameters... Choose LLMs.

Tools.Summary: MCP is integrated alongside Glean's own indexing via hybrid connectors, layered with knowledge graphs, specialized indexes, and an RL-trained enterprise-memory subsystem that refines tool-use strategies.

evidence.quote: At Glean, we treat MCP as complementary, combining it with our indexing system through hybrid connectors to achieve both real-time freshness and unified enterprise understanding.
Enterprise memory at Glean uses reinforcement learning to find the optimal tool use strategies.
GPT-5 has pushed long-horizon reasoning forward, Claude remains the strongest on code and tool use, and Gemini Flash shows what's possible with extremely fast, low-latency inference.

Stakeholders.Summary: AI/ML, platform, and ranking engineers own LLM integration; customer agent builders also tune instructions and parameters using Glean's evaluation tools.

evidence.quote: Everyone should learn how to evaluate agents, not just because it builds confidence in agent quality, but because it teaches you how to best use your agent platform.

Others.Summary: Glean enforces zero-retention model agreements, a RAG architecture minimizing LLM data exposure, and alignment models that pre-scan write actions. Purpose-built AI safeguard models achieve 97.8% / 93.5% / 94.3% accuracy on prompt injection, toxic content, and malicious code; a security dashboard provides full violation context for tracing.

evidence.quote: Zero-retention agreements with model providers ensure your data is never stored or used for model training.
That's why we added protection against agents veering off scope, using alignment models (beta) that pre-scan every write action before it executes.
Customers get single-tenant connectors, enforced data permissions, and a RAG architecture that minimizes LLM data exposure.
Glean achieves 97.8% accuracy on prompt injection detection, 93.5% accuracy on toxic content detection, and 94.3% on malicious code detection on leading benchmarks.
By fine-tuning using publicly available datasets relevant to enterprise scenarios, our models are better equipped to identify and mitigate enterprise-specific risks.
